and it now delivers.

Where AI360 stands this week, in plain terms: what has been earned, what it costs to run, who is using it, and what went wrong and how we found it.

Where we are

Someone can arrive at AI360, create an account, do real work, choose a plan, pay with a Ghanaian card or Mobile Money, and return to an active subscription. We have proved that whole path with real money — and as of today, a person can also walk away with a finished video.

11accounts created. None since 14 August.
GH₵125collected. One subscription active.
Yesvideo generation now works end to end.
Today's milestone: the studio delivered.

A four-second cinematic clip was generated, saved and played back from a real account. The same run confirmed the credit hold settled correctly at the quoted price. This was the last unproven promise in the product, and it is now closed.

The one sentence that matters

The hard engineering is largely behind us; the demand question is entirely ahead of us. The platform can take payment, measure usage, recover from its own failures and account honestly for what it spends. It has eleven accounts and one payment. Every remaining question is about whether people in Accra will use it and pay for it — and none of those can be answered by building more.

Money

What we earn on what we sell

Customers buy credits, either bundled in a monthly plan or as a one-off top-up. A credit costs us about GH₵0.26 in AI and processing charges. Here is what one sells for.

What the customer buysPriceCreditsCost to us per creditReal cost to usWe keep
Everyday plan (monthly)GH₵125120GH₵0.26GH₵31.2075%

Top-ups (one-off)GH₵50–20040–185GH₵0.26GH₵10.40–48.1076–79%

Even if a subscriber used every credit their plan includes, an Everyday subscription costs us about GH₵31 against GH₵125 collected. Top-ups are deliberately dearer per credit than a plan, so nobody is ever better off avoiding a subscription.

What we actually spend

Total AI cost for everything the product has ever done is about GH₵21 — roughly $1.40. That figure is now trustworthy, which it was not last week: our own records had overstated it fifty-fold because a background check was counting the same job over and over. Correcting it matters, because that number is what pricing decisions are made from.

Video pricing: we were quietly charging everyone the top rate
Before Every video used the most expensive engine, at about GH₵20 of credits per four-second clip. A cheaper engine was available and simply never offered to customers.
Now Customers choose, and each option shows its own price before they pick it — the number was previously invisible until the confirmation step. Clips can also be 4, 6 or 8 seconds, priced by the second. A quick 8-second clip costs less than a 4-second best-quality one. We keep a healthy margin on every option.

Users and adoption

Eleven accounts, all from our own circle, and no new ones since 14 August. That is not a fault in the product — we simply have not started telling anyone about it.

Two honest conclusions. First, the hole in the middle of the funnel is now closed — people can take a finished video away, which until today they could not. Second, we still cannot say whether anyone comes back, because we do not measure it. That is being added, and it is the next thing worth knowing.

What went wrong, and how we found it

Three faults surfaced this week. All three were the kind that look fine from the outside, which is the kind worth taking seriously.

1 · Finished work was being thrown away
What happened Every image and video the product ever made — seven attempts — was created correctly and then lost, because the place finished files are saved was never switched on for the live server. Videos sat on "Rendering…" forever. Images looked like they worked because they display from a temporary copy that is never kept.
What we did Found the cause in production's own records rather than by guesswork. The setting is now in place, the lost clip was recovered and delivered, and a fresh render has since been generated and saved successfully. The product also now fails honestly: if finished work cannot be saved, the person is told and their credits are returned rather than being left waiting.
2 · The homepage promised what a visitor could not have
What happened Three of the four things the homepage invited a new visitor to try required an account. Clicking the main button produced an error message with a reference code as their very first experience of AI360 — while the page said "Start free, no card".
What we did The free options now lead, and anything needing an account says so before it is clicked. Clicking the button with an empty box now answers a real question instead of doing nothing useful.
3 · Everything was a quarter too small to read
What happened Nearly half the text on the site was smaller than 12 pixels, some as small as 7. The product looked noticeably better when zoomed in — because zoom was compensating for a real design defect.
What we did Every text size raised on a measured curve, with a minimum floor. Checked at five screen sizes from phone to large desktop. Reading lines are now a comfortable length, and the phone keyboard no longer zooms the page.
